utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Crncalo. I hope you had a good rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for asking. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, it's for you to continue to cross-examine, but before you start, given that you already spent about 40 minutes -- half an hour, 26 minutes I was told, yesterday, I would expect you to conclude your cross-examination today, given that we are not sitting tomorrow. I could also expect that you could finish much before that. So can I ask how much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. I'm having a little problem with the computer, although all the parameters seem to be in order. But anyway, I asked for five hours for this witness because it's a witness from the main town in Republika Srpska, the war time capital where the state authorities were located. And there's some significant things in his statement, and I think that we can shed light on a lot of matters. I value the witness's co-operation, but I think it would be a good idea if I were given sufficient time not to have to rush through things, to make my questions clear so we can get short answers and clear answers. Before I begin, with your permission, I would like to say two or three things briefly. First of all, I have given up on the Defence document that we mentioned previously because it is going to crop up fairly frequent in this courtroom, and I don't want to upset Mr. Crncalo again because it has to do with Markale. So I'd like to avoid that, and I'll use the document with other witnesses. So it's not essential that we present it during this witness's testimony. The second point that I'd like to raise is this: It was only subsequently that I understood the importance of your guide-lines and your advice. So let me explain how the matter stands at present. If I say "all right" or "very well," it's not "right" or "okay." When I say "dobro," I just say, "Well, fine, I'm not going to insist." So that would be one of the linguistic problems and discrepancies that we're going to come across, and I'm going to point them out as they crop up. And, of course, you're free to ask me, although I'm not testifying, whether I say, "dobro," "yes, right," or whether I use this phrase, whether I accept it or given up on further insistence when I say, "dobro, right, fine." I must say I'm a little envious of Mr. Tieger because he has umpteen associates and helpers, and I was wondering if I could get an extra assistant because the material is vast and when Mr. Robinson comes back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I believe our interpreters can properly interpret whatever you say, and please start your cross-examination and try to conclude during the first half of the third session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, don't worry about a misinterpretation of what I said. We won't assume that you agree with a factual matter that's been attested to by a witness unless you specifically say that you agree with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphones please be switched on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like us to go through the first part of your statement. You were born in Radacici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's a village that takes its name from a part of the population living there; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But are there people with the surname Radacic living in Radacici?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's the surname Radaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, I think there are people with the surname Radacic too?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the village is called Radacici, but there's not a surname Radacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But is there a family called Radaca?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You worked at Korana at the military post 883 which means that that was military industry; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the -- that the factory producing special vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Radacici department and branch of the repair and maintenance factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's where the maintenance was carried out for the Yugoslav People's Army vehicles, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, motor vehicles were maintained there and repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian vehicles first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the factory was a military one, and there was this military post number?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you start working in that factory?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1965, I worked for four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you transferred to Zrak; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I did my Yugoslav People's Army service, and once I completed my service in the JNA, I started working for the Zrak company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is Zrak, in part, a military factory too?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That means that you had very good military characteristics?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's up to others to say. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you didn't have any problems in transferring from one army factory to another?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I arrived there wasn't a work post open when I had completed my military service and was looking for a job, but when I looked for a job in Zrak, I was able to find one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to the part of your statement which refers to the events of 1990 and 1991. So I'll just briefly summarise and repeat. You weren't a member of the SDA but you shared their ideals and ideology and you probably voted for them, although you didn't have to say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a sympathiser, but I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters are asking you to put a pause between the question and the answer. Could you bear that in mind, Mr. Crncalo, as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Yes, they're quite right, the interpreters are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 of your statement, you say that it was sometime in 1991 in the Muslim community that you started to notice some changes in the Serb population's attitude, and then you went on to say that you had in mind open speeches and references to Kosovo, Serbian historical events, and so on. And that -- well, let's deal with Kosovo first, this reference to Kosovo. Is that the first time that the Serbs talked about Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in Pale there isn't a separate Muslim community. The Pale municipality, the urban part of it, encompassed all citizens living in Pale and the Pale municipality. Pale was a whole, one entity. And in 1991, and especially in 1992, when the events took place which we all know about, there were frequent demonstrations. Columns were being formed made up of the Serb male population and bottles of brandy were held and the slogan that they shouted was, Kosovo, Kosovo, we're not going to let Kosovo go. There were flags too, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in another paragraph, it says the relationship towards your Muslim community --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Crncalo, given that Mr. Karadzic is putting questions about the paragraphs of your statement, would you like to have your statement in front of you? My understanding is that there is a translation of this. I checked it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There is a translation of this particular statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would like to have the statements in Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in e-court, Exhibit 733. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the Muslim community, I picked up from paragraph 10 in your statement, you used the term. Now, my question was: Was that the first time that you saw Serbs talking about Kosovo in 1991, or in previous decades and years were they taken up with the subject of Kosovo and were there demonstrations about Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Pale municipality, this never happened before 1990 -- 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember that the crisis in Kosovo took place, first of all in 1968, that was the first crisis, and the next wave was in 1971, and the third was in 1981, one year after Tito's death. Then from that time onwards, there was a permanent crisis involving Kosovo and over Kosovo, and every Yugoslav leadership and Presidency after Tito's death dealt with the topic of Kosovo. And this was particularly marked in 1988 and 1989. And that from the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1989, for instance, the Serbs went to attend a rally in Kosovo and there were a million and a half Serbs there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you're going back to history and asking me questions about history, but I'll give you this answer. As to the events about Kosovo, yes, I did learn about them from the electronic media and from the press. That's the first point. Secondly, I knew that policemen were designated to go to Kosovo, probably to keep law and order there. And now as to other activities that the population, the civilians, were shouting slogans, Kosovo, and defending Kosovo in Pale municipality, that did not happen until the war -- until these preparations for war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't belabour the point, but I'd like to remind you and to hear your opinion to this: The Kosovo crisis was the nucleus of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's leave Kosovo issue and come to our issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, you go on to say that this was unsettling, the Serb nationalist flags had an unsettling effect on you. Could you describe that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the flag has the four-S sign on it, and as soon as the flag was raised in Pale, things started going downhill. Inter-human relations were no longer the same. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what you describe is a religious flag, in fact, which has a cross and the three C scrolls, otherwise it's a tricolour, red, white, blue?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was this flag that was carried at the time that I'm talking about. The tricolour was to appear later on, I'm referring to the other type of flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the killings on the 1st of March, 1992, in the wedding party in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I lived in Pale. I did not live in Sarajevo, so I wasn't present. Yes, I did hear about it. I heard that something had happened in Sarajevo, that a killing had taken place, but I was not in Sarajevo myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you weren't in Kosovo either, but it was unsettling you said for you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was unsettling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear what the killer of the people in the wedding party, Gardovic said on television, why he killed them in Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll remind you. Perhaps this will jog your memory. He said the wedding party was carrying a Serb flag. Now, I want to ask you whether you remember that the Serbian religious flag was always carried in -- at weddings, and even during the time of the Turks, from the beginning of the nineteenth century when the flag was espoused, and it was different from the Russian flag, and that Serb wedding parties were allowed to display their religious flags in all systems, including the communist system. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told this -- I have given a statement to this august Trial Chamber. I told them what I lived through, what I experienced. And now you're asking me, most probably it has some value for you, but you're asking me about quite different matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a copy in the witness's language of the amalgamated statement. Perhaps the usher could provide the witness with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could it be passed on to the witness. Mr. Crncalo, I think I can understand how you feel, but if you can answer yes and no, you can simply do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that it was also disturbing to the Serbs to see that their flag bothers someone so much that they are prepared to kill?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly there are persons like that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the ethnic composition in Pale, I have information that there were 27 per cent Muslims or around 4 and a half thousand, almost 5.000, and the rest were Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information from the time of the elections was the Muslims were 33 per cent. I didn't check it, I just read this, around 5.000. Now, which of the two is correct, it's up to someone else to judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have the election results and we can look them up. Is it the case that the Serbian Democratic Party governed on its own or shared power with the Muslim party and would have shared it with the Croatian Democratic Union if there had been any Croats?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They divided power as it suited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it part of the agreement that applied to the entire republic regarding proportional representation in the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a politician, although I had once been nominated to be a delegate and didn't accept, and I cannot answer this question. I cannot say either yes or no. It's up to the people who actually occupied these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Crncalo, if you say that the Serbian Democratic Party divided the power as it suited it, it sounds like diktat. I want to remind you that at the level of the republic through the government, Assembly, the Presidency, down to the last municipality, one single principle was accomplished; namely, that all the three nations, through their political parties, participate in government in proportion to their strength and in keeping with an agreement reached at the level of the republic. That's how it worked. If there were 27 per cent Muslims in Pale and 27 per cent Serbs in Stari Grad, that's what -- that's the kind of proportionality that was applied.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If what you say is true, then why were our telephones cut off?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that issue later. You confirmed yesterday - and it's in the statement as well - that the deputy president of the municipality was Hamed Palo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention him at all yesterday. Hamed Palo was, indeed, appointed in 1992. Now, how long he stayed in that position, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any Muslims in the Executive Board of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you a moment ago that the composition of the government in the municipality Pale was not nearly my main interest with all that was going on, so I can neither confirm nor deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crncalo, but I have to clarify this because with your side comments you suggest that this was not so, and I want to remind you that in every municipality, if it was composed of all the three ethnic groups, they shared power depending on which ethnic community was in the majority. And the gentlemen sitting in this courtroom do not know about our relationships, and I cannot leave this impression that you create by your swipes to stand, namely, that we took power and divided it as we wanted.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I am answering as best I know. I have made an oath, not only to this Court but also before God. I want to speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say in paragraph 13 -- you speak about St. Djordje's day, the Serbian holiday, the 6th of May. You say Seselj came and stationed Chetniks on a mountain near Novak's cave. Is St. Djordje's day only a Serbian holiday, isn't it also a Roma holiday?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any Roma living in Pale, I really don't. But I know that many families celebrated St. Djordje's day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You heard certainly about the St. Djordje's wake. It was taken over from an earlier tradition. Was it just St. Djordje's wake that Seselj came for?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're asking me about is St. Djordje's day a Serbian holiday. It's not the 1st May wake. It was celebrated in the Sarajevo municipality of Ilidza. St. Djordje's day is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move forward because we can't agree about this. Do you know that Seselj has some Muslim members in his own party, in the top leadership, descendents of late Mehmet Spaho?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a Chetnik leader during the Second World War, which means a Royalist, who was not condemned like Tito by the Western allies, had in his headquarters a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't even born then and neither were you, and you're asking me about Draza Mihajlovic and his ADC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, your statement is full of resentment towards Chetniks. I don't know whether you're talking about Chetniks proper or you mean that every Serb is a Chetnik. But Chetniks were actually recognised by some Western countries as anti-fascists, Draza Mihajlovic was decorated by the American government. He had a very prominent Muslim assistant in his headquarters, just like Seselj has Mr. Spaho in his own party?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would you call people in Pale who were carrying the flag with the skull and bones under a fur hat? Isn't that a Chetnik emblem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's move on to real issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said you found the behaviour of Serbs in 1991 at Christmas disturbing, that there was more shooting than usual?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was shooting. We couldn't even sleep there was so much shooting, especially from dusk until late at night. It almost didn't stop all night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you blamed it on the new government and Malko Koroman?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, do you know when the new government actually took over after the elections? Do you agree that the new government was formed in the way that I will describe now? The Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina was set up on the 20th December, and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed on the 30th of January, three weeks after the Serbian Christmas.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political parties took power actually before all these Assemblies were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It takes a couple of months after the elections to form a government. Do you know when the Serb Christmas is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7 January.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have a map of Pale and the environs? P19122, it's a Prosecution exhibit. P9122 or 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, the correct number is 19112. This is a map which the accused requested that we provide them with, and we co-operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, do you see this map of Pale municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in Brdarici, Praca, Kamenica, and Renovica, the population is majority Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Probably in the north, in Bogovici as well. But do you remember who controlled Pale municipality during the war? Were Serbs in control of Renovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that much better than I do. They controlled Renovica. Serb troops moved in on that part of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's not debate this. Please answer the question: Did Serbs control the Renovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me certain things. After the attack on Renovica, they didn't control it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we control Praca?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is now Praca the seat of the Muslim municipality of Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the Dayton Accords when the territory was divided up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So according to Dayton maps, Praca became part of the Federation and became seat of the Muslim municipality of Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that before the war we proposed that all municipalities in which there are compact segments of one or another community be transformed into one or more -- into two or more municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not follow your political wrangling and meetings, but I did see what happened on the ground. Now, what you were trying to negotiate with the top leaders of other parties I was unable to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then we'll leave political topics aside. Let's go back to your statement where you talk about the way of life in Pale and how it all worked. You say in your statement that there were many refugees in Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, as a general matter, could I request the accused just to provide a paragraph number of the statement, and while I'm on my feet, when he refers to the accused's [sic] evidence which he gave yesterday, if he could provide a transcript page in accordance with the order for the conduct of trial, which Your Honours have handed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, you referred to the accused's evidence he gave yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think he meant to say the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Try to indicate the paragraph or page number's when you use them, when you put them to the witness. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like staying with the map to ask you whether you know where Cemerno is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard it, but I don't know where it is exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's towards Nisici "visoravan," plateau.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Vukasinovici are?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know people with surname Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, I mean the Vukasinovici village.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let's move on to paragraph 23 of your statement where you say that on the 3rd of March, 1992, that you were arrested. Were you arrested or detained?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can explain it any way you like, but I was seized by three reserve policemen and taken to the police station, and I was handcuffed. Now, you can comment about that any way you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't find those handcuffs in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were on my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were questioned there and then in the morning, finally, Mr. Malko Koroman took you and your neighbour back; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Crncalo, what happened to Serbs in Sarajevo who were found in possession of weapons, escorted by the police chief, as you were, or they disappeared never to be seen again?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the police station in Pale, they have my human qualities. They know about me, what kind of person I was. So most probably they returned me because of that. They knew them -- the man I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, just for clarity, I'd like to remind you that Mr. Crncalo, in his statement, para 23, in the middle of it, he clearly stated that: "At the police station, I was handcuffed and interrogated by Hrusum." Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. That's why I need the statements in Serbian, at least the statements if I can't have the transcripts in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have it in front of you on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, but I didn't have it earlier on for me to be able to mark that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, on the 3rd of March, 1992, did Yugoslavia exist and Bosnia-Herzegovina exist, whose foreign minister was Alija Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Yugoslavia, the one that existed at one time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer. Let me answer. And the parties took over the -- once the parties took over power and authority, that Yugoslavia no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we have Defence exhibit 1D801, please. 1D801, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll go through a number of documents quickly, and they'll show us what the situation was like at Pale. We have a news agency news item, saying that: "The wave of refugees, on the entire territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, was growing from one day to the next." And here we see that the number of refugees at Sokolac and Pale cannot be determined with any precision. Now, do you remember that there were as many refugees as there were local inhabitants and sometimes more refugees than local inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any statistics of the influx of people coming into Pale, but, yes, there were lots of people arriving.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D816 now, please -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The previous document was dated the 10th of April, 1992. So four days after the war began, Pale was full of refugees. 1D816 is the next document I'd like us to look at. You have the Serbian version in front of you, Mr. Crncalo, and the date there is the 19th of May. And this is what it says: "A large number of refugees from Sarajevo are arriving in Pale today. At the present moment, 2.500 families registered with the Pale Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff at Pale is moving them into surrounding cottages, but, as they are all full, they will be moving in with families from Pale and some are heading towards Belgrade. "Currently the Crisis Staff for the accommodation of refugees, along with the representatives of the Red Cross have begun distributing food, although there's less and less food here at present." Now, was Pale a sort of weekend resort for the people of Sarajevo before the war?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know what kind of neighbourhood and settlement it was. All I know is that the refugees poured into Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, do you mean to say that you don't know that Pale was a holiday resort with weekend cottages for the population of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, before the war; but what happened after the war I can't say or during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that before the war there were a lot of weekend cottages there and that the Crisis Staff filled up these cottages, accommodated the refugees in them, and then sent them to move in with families. Did you take any refugees in, your family?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why? Why not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can answer that. Nobody offered -- made the offer, and even if they did ask me to do so, I would have had to take them in, but nobody asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody had to. It was on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we look at 1D817 next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please bear that in mind that we set up a rule regarding the exhibit to deal with it every time when you've used it. So if you are going to tender those things, you should raise it, and after hearing from the Prosecution, we will rule on it, we will make a decision. So you are minded to tender those 8 -- those two documents, a news clipping from a Serbian news agency, 801 and 816?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I'm getting used to it, but my skills haven't been honed out yet. Yes, I would like to tender these Defence documents into evidence, 1D801 and 1D816. And now I would like to call up 1D817.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, there's no objection to their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will admit them. What's the number of them?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1D801 will be Exhibit D8; and 65 ter number 1D816 will be Exhibit D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you have before you a document dated the 20th of May. It refers to refugees in Pale, and the last paragraph says: "The Red Cross has also appealed to the local population to take in some of the people who are temporarily residing in the hall of the municipality, if they are able to do so," which means there are no longer any cottages and weekend homes free. Do you agree that that was what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, another paragraph says that some people were not able to be accommodated at Pale and they went on to Belgrade, Cacak, and Serbia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see that, but I don't know that they went on towards Cacak and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D -- or before I ask for the next document, I'd like to tender this document into evidence, 1D817.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be number 10. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to call up 1D807.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have it before you, Mr. Crncalo. It's a news agency item dated the 17th of April, and already on the 17th of April, there were still 2.000 families, refugee families, at Pale. And we received this from the centre -- social services centre of the municipality. And it says that from this same centre news has arrived that today the first shipment of food has started for those registered with the staff for accommodating the refugees, family packages and food for children are being distributed, which was received, in part, from the International Red Cross and UNICEF of the Serbian municipality of Pale, and more packages are expected from UNICEF and the Serbian humanitarian society called Dobrotvor.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, how can I answer questions like that when I have absolutely no knowledge of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you accept that there was this problem of feeding such a large number of refugees?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the Pale municipality had in terms of resources. All I saw was convoys coming in, lots of convoys, full of corn and APCs in between, and they were moving towards the silos where the corn was being stored. I do know that, but as to the other things you're asking me about, I have absolutely no idea about any of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up -- or before I do, I'd like to tender this document into evidence, 1D807.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There's no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have document ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's admitted and that's D11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the convoys. When did you see them, Mr. Crncalo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the war some food reserves were collected; right? Is that what that means?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where it came from, where the trailer trucks came from and where the APCs that were mixed up amongst them. I don't know where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have 1D824 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document with the date the 21st of May, and it's a news agency item which says that there are already 15.000 registered refugees in Pale, and it goes on to say that it is impossible to house all of them. But would you focus on the last paragraph where it says: "Food reserves are being -- are nearly exhausted, what is particularly needed is flour, oil, sugar, and children's food." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't see -- it doesn't say, "decija hrana," but, "djecija hrana," meaning children's food, with different accents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours this is a linguistic matter. You can forget about that, whether it's the Ekavian or Jekavian. But, anyway, I'd like to tender this document, 1D824.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From your position, I take it all the "SRNA" agency news clippings are not objected to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as D12. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I have Defence document 1D805 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's rather a poor copy, more legible in English, but I'll read it out in Serbian for us, the two of us, Mr. Crncalo, for you in Bosnian and me in Serbian: "Life in the region of the municipality of Pale is slowly returning to normal, after it has been subjected to the most intense war attacks over the past several days. The Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Pale has issued a decision to allow elementary schools in Pale, Mokrom, and Praca to reopen starting tomorrow." Is Praca a Muslim village in Pale municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Praca isn't a village. It's a local commune including surrounding villages. It wasn't a purely Muslim or a purely Serbian village. There were more Serbs in Praca than Muslims in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put something to you now and you can tell me whether you agree or not, that in addition to the reopening of the schools, already on the 12th of April, that is to say eight days, a week after the war attacks broke out and "opstina" Pale was under fire as well, the school was open in Praca and Mokrom, which is a purely Serb village, and that a public transport route towards Praca was also reopened. It doesn't say that here but we can find that piece of information. Do you gray with that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the reopening of the school, but I do know about the reopening of the bus route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who attacked Pale municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that when from Pale municipality the Serb units attacked the local commune of Renovica and Zepa, as far as I know too, they attacked that. But who attacked Pale municipality, where I moved around, I didn't see that the Pale municipality was attacked at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I wanted to ask you was: Who were the warring sides? Who could have attacked Pale, because there weren't any Croats there which means that it was the Muslim forces which attacked Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pale municipality borders on the Stari Grad-Sarajevo municipality. So how many units from the Stari Grad, old town, municipality took control of Pale municipality, you know that better than me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I would like to tender this exhibit too, 1D805. Since we have your agreement in principle, can we move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's admitted as D13 and move on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to call up 1D813.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, were there any weapons among the Muslim population in Praca and in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these weapons were all registered at the police station in Pale. It was all hunting and sports weapons. There was no other arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were no automatic weapons that were smuggled in?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And every one of us in Pale who had a hunting weapon had to turn it in to the police station because Malko Koroman, chief of police, demanded that all the weapons owned by Croats and Muslims be surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of Imam Fazlo Gljiva?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Senaid Memic from Hrasnica, who brought a large number of weapons for Muslims in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that, and he couldn't have passed through all the check-points to bring in any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Malko Koroman make an announcement on the radio, or otherwise, that weapons should be brought into the police station?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Pale a Sarajevo suburb municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a suburb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it was part of Sarajevo municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, could I draw your attention to the document on the screen dated 28th April. It says: "As a result of a successful operation by the employees of the public security station in Pale, most Muslims from Praca handed over their weapons today. Automatic rifles, which had been distributed with the mediation of the Praca Imam Fazlo Gljiva were handed over to the authorities. These weapons had arrived in Praca through channels used by Senaid Memic from Hrasnica. This well-known Muslim extremist armed members of the Muslim community throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and from that shipment, 20 automatic rifles arrived in the Praca region." Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these weapons were legally distributed at the police station of Pale to reserve policemen, and those who couldn't muster the courage to bring this rifle and uniform to the police station were returned otherwise. I personally took two rifles from two reserve policemen and turned them over at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about weapons that people are issued with when they go on an exercise, be they reserve policemen or reserve soldiers, they get gas masks and uniforms and weapons, and they take it all home.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it used to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was in keeping with the Tito's doctrine of armed population?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how long they kept -- they got to keep the uniforms and the equipment, I mean registered reserve policemen. These were not distributed to other regular people. And when this announcement came, some of these reserve policemen did not have the courage to bring it in themselves to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree about the reserve policemen, but were you ever called up to do an exercise as a military reservist?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that time would you also take the uniform and sometimes the weapon home?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I could not drive an armoured vehicle back to my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but infantrymen could take weapons home, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document, 1D813, and may I now call up 1D855, a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 813 would be admitted as D14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see that these weapons concerned were not army issue or government issue. They were smuggled weapons, contraband weapons. This talks about the conduct of Senaid Memic from Hrasnica. That same person was mentioned in the news item of the agency "SRNA." And here is his statement, or rather, the Official Note on his arrest. I quote: "In the period between September 1991 to my arrest, I had for the purposes of the SDA in Bosnia and Sandzak purchased, imported, and distributed around 5.000 automatic rifles of various types and around 1.400.000 rounds." Where is Sandzak? You know but the gentlemen in the courtroom don't.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it's bordering on Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not part of Bosnia. You asked where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have it on the transcript that part of Sandzak is in Montenegro and part of Sandzak is in Serbia. The witness actually said it. Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sandzak is partly in Montenegro and partly in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's continue with the text: "I did all this in co-operation with SDA activists on the ground, and following orders by certain leaders of the SDA party." "On the ground," do you see that in the text?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if I see it, it doesn't matter. But look who distributed all these weapons to the Serbian people without any fee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this in exchange for a fee?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know because I didn't buy anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go on: "My closest ties in this job were with Cengic, who normally acts as the technical secretary of the SDA. All these dealings of mine were known to all leaders of the political top echelon of the SDA party, beginning with Alija Izetbegovic, through Omer Behmen, Rusmir Mahmutcehajic, and others, as well as certain officials of the MUP of the SR Bosnia-Herzegovina; the MUP Minister, Alija Delimustafic; Deputy Staff Minister, Mirsad Srebrenkovic; Jusuf Pusina; Bakir Alispahic; Kemal Sabovic; Munir Alibabic, as well as some other heads of the SJB throughout Bosnia ..." Do you, as a sympathiser of the SDA party, and a man who is familiar with the SDA on the ground, the leadership with whom this man co-operated in distributing weapons, were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am a man of integrity. You are asking me about people who are involved in arms smuggling, or smuggling as such. I was never involved in anything like and never would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you said in paragraph 12 that you know the leadership of the SDA. These are not smugglers. This is the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is about the Ministry of the Interior. These are the Muslim senior officers in the police force of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bakir Alispahic, who is an Iranian spy planted by the Iranian intelligence service. This concerns the Muslim leadership taking advantage of common resources to arm one ethnic community. Maybe you didn't know the top leadership at republic level?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are making an extensive comment rather than asking a question. The witness can't deal with that and it's not evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he can confirm that these were prominent and important people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer now. First of all, you mentioned a smuggler, and then you mentioned some other people, and then you asked me whether I know the smuggler and these other people. The politicians, I saw on television, just as I saw your own associates on TV. As for this smuggler, I've never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the people on local level whom you knew.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document. This is an Official Note -- rather, a statement given to the police, 1D855.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, we object to the admission of that document. The principal reason is that as your offers -- as Your Honours ruled yesterday, the accused will have ample opportunity to use the 92 bis and 92 ter regime during his Defence case to submit witness statements. And this is essentially witness statement. Now, if the accused chooses to submit this particular witness statement, I'd like to reserve the right to make further submissions at that time as to the reliability of this statement, the circumstances in which it was taken, the authorities which took this statement, and the question as to whether it is a true reflection of this person's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say one thing. This document is corroborated by a news agency report that the agency received at the police. These documents go hand in hand. That other document mentions the "hodza," or in other words Imam, and also Senaid Memic who distributed arms for the needs of the highest Muslim leadership. This was an official questioning by an official authority and it's accompanied by a witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, as we made it clear yesterday, we will not admit a statement of third parties unless it satisfies the requirements of the Rules, Rule 92 ter or Rule 92 bis. Otherwise, on a separate -- the Prosecution may well be able to introduce hundreds, thousands of statements which corroborate with the Prosecution evidence. We will strictly apply this rule and most of the content was put to the witness, although he denied it or had no knowledge about it. So based upon that principle, we will not admit this. Please go on. That does not exclude you putting the content of the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Maybe I forgot to say that there is also a handwritten statement of this suspect, not only the typewritten version. I'd now like to call 1D818. We now see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 22 May 1992: "Drive to disarm Muslim paramilitaries in Praca and Renovica." Let me remind you that you said that those people, who wanted to, brought their weapons voluntarily to the police station, and the police did not need to go to their houses to collect them. Let's see what the document says. So those who wanted to, brought their weapons in. Were there people who didn't want to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I lived in Pale; they lived in Praca. I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said today, and I'll look for a reference in the transcript, that Pale was one whole. That's page 6 of today's transcript, that Pale was one whole, one municipality.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I now answer? Pale was one whole, in terms of territory, but I once tried to go to Radacici where I was born. I came up to the Famos factory, when I was intercepted by two soldiers wearing reserve army uniforms. One of them trained his rifle at me, almost touching my stomach, while the other one asked me to produce my ID. I was afraid to reach into my pocket, fearing that the other one might think I'm trying to remove the gun. And then they asked me, Where are you going? I said I wanted to sow potatoes. And they, Open the back of the car. There were tools, agricultural tools. There was a sack of potatoes. There was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Did you mention this in a previous statement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was in the spring?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the police operation of disarming underway at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date in the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 22nd May.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened earlier, and that's why I said that Pale was one single whole, but when that happened, I realised that things were no longer as they used to be. You can't move around in Pale just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let's focus on this document now. There was this drive to disarm the population, and this was after the voluntary -- partial voluntary surrendering of weapons. Now, reading this news agency report it says: "Today the members of the active reserve unit of the public security station in Pale engaged in an effort to disarm the Muslim paramilitary forces in Praca and Renovica neighbourhoods with a majority Muslim population." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember Malko's statement on television, and you could see tears in his eyes. This is what he said, his very words, Unfortunately war has come to Pale municipality. Those were his very words and I remember them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did he say that with respect to the killing of Goran Kablar and Rade Tosic, his policeman, and the wounding of five MUP members in Renovica in this action to gather up weapons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but not -- that wasn't collecting up weapons. It was an action of some kind in the territory similar to what had happened in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document, 1D818, into evidence as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as D15, and we will have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, before you break, one quick matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Court will be aware that witness scheduling is a delicate balance between the convenience -- burden on the witnesses and the need to move the process forward. In that regard, if the Court is minded to provide some estimate of the cross-examination time for the fourth witness, it will assist, or the Court may be content for the Prosecution to make its scheduling judgements based on events to date. But I wanted to bring that issue to the attention of the Court and ask for whatever assistance the Court was minded to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The immediate question is whether to release the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not the next witness at this moment. It's for scheduling down the line, anticipating how many witnesses and which witnesses will be heard before this Court next week; and, therefore, which additional witnesses need -- may need to be present or whose arrival may be deferred until the week following, for example. So it's the knock-on effect for the upcoming witnesses of the length of cross-examination for the fourth witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You tendered your anticipated time for examination-in-chief, as did the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we have the same material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And if the Court wishes us to base it on that we, will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will see what we can do. Thank you. For 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For record, the resumption of the second session has been delayed due to some technical difficulties which has been resolved. And we'll take the next break just for 20 minutes, and I -- as I said to you, Mr. Karadzic, so let's try to conclude this witness's evidence by today and then I think there's no point to keep the next witness waiting for his evidence. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I'd just like to say that my entire preparation was in electronic mode and I had expected to be able to link up here with this computer, but I did have a backup option and I sent three CD-ROMs to Mr. Sladojevic with my preparations. But we didn't receive either, we weren't provided with either. So I was handicapped inasmuch as I did not have the necessary preparations and material that I thought I could use on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Crncalo, in the previous document, 818, it says in the last paragraph there, after what you said, that it was with tears in his eyes that Malko Koroman said, after the killing of these two policemen and the wounding of others, the action is still in progress, and the MUP of Pale is calling on all the Muslims in these neighbourhoods to hand-over their weapons in a peaceful way and to refrain from causing any further bloodshed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this -- this is already an exhibit. I'd like to call up Defence exhibit 1D825 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's on our screens. I'll read out what it says: "In this evening's informative programme of Serbian television, Malko Koroman, head of the MUP of Pale, posed an ultimatum to the armed Muslims in Pale municipality demanding that by the next day, the 23rd of May, by 3.00 p.m., they hand in their weapons. "The ultimatum followed an attack by the Muslim paramilitaries in Renovica on a MUP patrol and members of the MUP, Goran Kablar and Rade Tosic, were killed and five other persons were wounded." The date is the 22nd of May, and after those tears he began functioning as the chief and issued an ultimatum. Do you remember that? I'm sure you do.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, but that wasn't the sequence of events. The Serbs attacked the Muslims in Renovica. The Muslims didn't intend to attack anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, they went there to collect up the weapons. How many Muslims and how many Serbs were killed in that action?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, two Serbs were killed and I don't know how many wounded, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And not a single Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you. I'm saying that not a single Muslim was killed.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they caused -- it was the Serb soldiers that caused the conflict by going there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender ID825 into evidence, please. I think we have an agreement in principle by the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit D16.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to call up 1D820, please. We have the Serbian version on our screens and the English one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date is the 23rd of May, that is to say the following day. "Muslims return their weapons," that is the heading. And it says: "After yesterday's ultimatum given by Malko Koroman, the chief of the police station in Pale, for all armed Muslims from Pale to return their weapons by today by 1300 [as interpreted] hours, we have learned that the operation of returning weapons is in progress. By 1700 hours, over 300 pieces of firing weapons from around 30 local villages have been returned to the police station in Pale. It is expected that there will be a lot more because the operation is still underway." Let's remind ourselves. First of all, there was one wave of voluntary surrender of weapons, then the police went round to round up the remaining weapons. Two policemen were killed, then came the ultimatum, and then the second wave of voluntary surrender of weapons took place.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's how it was, why wasn't anybody killed in Pale on the Serb or Muslim side, why not in Praca, why not in Podgrab? Because there was no coercion needed. The announcement was made and the people returned their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we agree on that point, but why didn't the people from Renovica return their weapons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because after that day for two or three years, maybe throughout the war, nobody dared live in Renovica. Why? Because Renovica was fired at by the artillery from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D820 tendered into evidence as have been the other documents? Thank you. And I'd now like to call up 1D822.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is Exhibit D17.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D822 is the next number. It wasn't recorded in the transcript. That's the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date is the 24th of May there, and the heading is: "Returning of weapons underway." Was there any illegal -- did the population have any illegal weapons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. All I know is about the weapons that were registered and how do I know that? Well, I know that because I was a huntsman, I liked the sport of hunting, and I socialised only with people who had -- who were in lawful possession of weapons, hunting weapons, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see what it says in the first paragraph. It says: "Responding to the ultimatum given two days ago by Malko Koroman, the chief of the police station in Pale, the Muslims from this municipality are returning more and more weapons by the hour." And then the second paragraph goes on to say: "Of course it is not without merit to believe that besides the weapons listed, there are illegally acquired weapons, whose owners have not yet come forward to the police station in Pale. As a reminder, in the recent action in Renovica, police officers confiscated one sniper; a double-barrel handmade rifle, which uses a high-calibre ammunition of 12 millimetres; four handguns; and a number of bottles with Molotov cocktails." Do you see what it says there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, what was this Molotov cocktail used for? Was that a hunting weapon?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have heard of Molotov cocktails, but I only saw something like on television, never in real life, so I really can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence as well, please, 1D822.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D18.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to call up 1D826 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have the document now. Mr. Crncalo, you said that people fled from Renovica. Tell me this, please, were there Serbs living in Renovica as well?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a number of them, but very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did they have any problems with their Muslim neighbours after this crisis?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't live down there myself, but knowing what the situation was like before the war I don't assume they had any problems. They co-operated in all areas and had good relations. They were good neighbours, good friends, they socialised, they went to work together, their children went to the same schools together, there weren't any problems. But after this happened, I wasn't down there so I don't want to talk about the rumours I heard. I don't know that there were any problems among the population living around -- in and around Renovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have 1D826 in front of us now, and the heading there is: "The situation of displaced Serbian families from Renovica." This document was sent to the Municipal Assembly of Pale by the committee of Serbian villages from the Renovica local commune. And this was sent on the following day, that is to say on the 26th of June. However, it refers to events that took place on the 15th of May and onwards. And it says in the second paragraph: "After the 15th of May, 1992, immediately after the Serb forces had collected up the weapons from the members of the Muslim forces in Renovica and its local commune in a military action, the Muslim forces took revenge on the minority Serb population, killing four people of Serb ethnicity and destroying a large number of houses and outbuildings. Given the fact that the military and civilian authorities of Pale municipality did not protect the Serb population in Renovica in any way, these Serb families were displaced and have found temporary shelter in other villages in the municipality with a majority Serb population. They have left behind considerable property, both movable and immovable, which is now being looted. And the Serbs are finding it difficult to survive. To date, these families have not been taken care of or given appropriate accommodation. We hereby appeal to the authorities of Pale municipality personally to investigate the situation and to try to solve the existential question and the problem of the survival of the Serbs from Renovica in a just manner." And that was written on the 25th of June, 1992, sent by the villagers' committee. Now, I don't know if we have an addition to this letter on e-court. Anyway, you know that refugees did arrive from Renovica to Pale; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says at the beginning of this document, in line 2: "Immediately after the military action, immediately after the military action, events occurred in Renovica," the ones that you're describing now. But it didn't involve gathering up weapons. It was a military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, we have other documents from which we can see that the army involved the police to round up the weapons, to save the soldiers from having to do that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm just reading what it says in your document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. But we have the documents, we have Malko Koroman's statement explaining why he sent the policemen to do what they did, because the army asked the police to carry out this operation and he lost two policemen, two were killed, and five others were wounded. And then the Serb neighbours were killed, ordinary civilians who were neither in the army or the police force.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any of that. I'm telling you what I did. I said that I wasn't able to move around the urban part of Pale, and I'm a heavy smoker, let me tell you. But most of the time while I was in Pale, I didn't have any cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'd like to tender this document 1D826 into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Doraiswamy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's an addition to this document, it's still being translated, but, anyway, it's a table, a list of the Serbs from Renovica, Serb families from Renovica. And it says who fled to Pale to the urban area and what property they left behind: Brojnici, Skipina, Rajko; Risto Corovic; Sofija Purkovic, it's a whole list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I interrupt, Your Honour. Could I ask that the accused identify the number of this document on the list that was provided to us by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It was 1D827, the next document following on from the previous one. I've read this out Sofija Purkovic; Grozda; Corovic; Luka Kalajdzic; Milanko Mitrovic, that's from the village of Brojnici. And what they left behind was houses, sheds, bombs, 35 sheep, one cow, one pig, and a lot of chickens, and he, this first person, went to stay with his son, Dragan, at Pale. Everything else was burned. He doesn't know where his cattle and animals are, and a lot of other agricultural equipment. Then we have Risto Corovic, he left behind a house, two barns, a shed, 60 sheep, three cows, two horses, two pigs, chickens, and so on. All the other outbuildings and agricultural equipment was set fire to, including a tractor, a small TAM truck, a sowing machine, and so on. Tell me whether you know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm surprised to see that you don't have any data about how many Muslim males were arrested in Renovica and taken to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you tell us then.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know there were such people. I don't know what the number was, but I do know that they were beaten up and that three of them succumbed to their wounds and died as a result of the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, but let's see what these people, these Serbs from Renovica, suffered at the hands of their neighbours, Grozda, another woman left a house, a barn, a shed, ten sheep, her animals taken away. Luka Kalajdzic also left behind a barn, a shed, and a house, 15 sheep, two cows and two pigs and the outbuildings were set fire to, his animals taken away, and so on and so forth. For the next person, too; however, his cattle were not burnt, neither was his house. From the village of Jelak, we have Srdanovic, Gojko; Milja Srdanovic, she was an old woman. Then we have Ranko Sokolovic, those are the same Sokolovics that Mehmet-Pasa Sokolovic, the famous Turkish "fezija," [phoen] they were descendants of him, the same name, Sokolovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does Mr. Crncalo dispute this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just read, is this Jelak or Ilijak village?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The original says Jelak.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that village. I know about a village called Ilijak. Ilijak population did not need to be evacuated from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know Srdanovics, Pavlovics from Renovica, do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know Srdanovics, they are the most numerous. There are Removics as well, all of them except this old woman, and one person had their property burned, but I would like this document marked for identification because we are still awaiting translation. It's 1D827. But, in summary, there is Skipina, Corovic, Turkovic, three families, Corovic, Mitrovic, Srdanovic, Srdanovic again, Sokolovics, two --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
